title: How freight brokers explain value when a shipper wants a lower rate
seoTitle: Freight Rate Objections: Explaining Your Brokerage’s Value
searchIntent: How can a freight broker respond when a shipper says the rate is too high?
excerpt: Respond to freight rate objections by comparing shipment scope, capacity, communication and service responsibilities before discussing price.
takeaway: A useful rate conversation compares the work and commitments behind the number. Explain the service you can actually deliver.

sections.title: Acknowledge the comparison before defending the rate
paragraphs: A shipper asking for a lower rate is giving you information about the buying decision. Luis encourages brokers to understand that decision rather than immediately cutting the quote or arguing that service always matters more.

Ask what is being compared. A quoted price can look attractive while leaving equipment, timing, accessorials or the capacity commitment unclear. Clarifying those details makes the conversation specific.

sections.title: Compare equivalent shipment requirements
paragraphs: Confirm that both options address the same pickup and delivery expectations, equipment and handling requirements. A different scope can explain a different number without making either party dishonest.

Distinguish an indicative quote from a commitment to cover a defined shipment. Avoid accusing another provider of failure you cannot substantiate. Explain what your own quote includes and which conditions could change it.

sections.title: Connect service to the shipper’s work
paragraphs: Luis discusses the work created when capacity falls through or a shipment requires recovery. A customer may have to coordinate facilities, answer internal questions and find another truck while trying to perform their normal job.

Describe how your process addresses those tasks: confirming requirements, qualifying a carrier, communicating exceptions and following through on delivery. Do not claim you can eliminate every delay or guarantee an outcome you do not control.

sections.title: Know what a concession would change
paragraphs: Lowering a rate can be a legitimate decision when the costs, scope or commercial circumstances support it. It becomes a problem when every objection produces an automatic discount without examining the shipment economics.

Review the carrier cost and the work required before making a new commitment. If a lower figure depends on different timing or requirements, explain that trade-off. Avoid creating an expectation that the first quote was arbitrary.

sections.title: Distinguish gross profit from take-home income
paragraphs: The difference between the customer rate and carrier cost is not all personal income. The brokerage must support the work involved in obtaining, arranging and administering the shipment.

That internal reality helps you evaluate the opportunity, but it is not automatically a persuasive sales pitch. The customer needs a clear explanation of useful service, not a request to subsidize unexplained overhead.

sections.title: Close the conversation with a clear next step
paragraphs: Confirm whether the customer wants to proceed under the quoted scope, revise a requirement or revisit the opportunity later. Record what was agreed so operations can deliver the same service sales described.

Luis’s teaching is strongest when the value discussion stays practical. Show the process, be honest about the commitment and let the price conversation reflect the actual shipment rather than unsupported claims about competitors or industry failure rates.
